current: "Neodymium shares three valence electrons; its four unpaired 4f electrons stay on each atom and give strong magnetism in compounds."
corrected: "Neodymium shares three valence electrons; its three remaining unpaired 4f electrons stay on each atom and give strong magnetism in compounds."
source: Standard lanthanide metal bonding: Nd metal is trivalent, 4f3 (5d6s)3, the same 4f3 core as Nd3+ in Nd2Fe14B
reason: The free atom is 4f4 6s2. Sharing three valence electrons moves one 4f electron into the bonding band, so only three localized 4f electrons remain, not four. The sentence contradicts itself.

source: NUBASE2020; Wikipedia Isotopes of caesium: Cs-135 T1/2 = 1.33(19)x10^6 y
reason: 2.3 Myr is the older value. The current evaluated half-life, based on a 2019 measurement, is 1.33 Myr, about 40% shorter.

source: XENONnT 2022 (Phys. Rev. C 106, 024328); Wikipedia Xenon infobox: Xe-124 1.1x10^22 y
reason: 1.8x10^22 y is the first XENON1T 2019 result. The more precise 2022 measurement gives (1.1 +/- 0.2)x10^22 y, and that is now the value usually cited.

current: Neodymium shares three valence electrons; its four unpaired 4f electrons stay on each atom and give strong magnetism in compounds.
corrected: "Neodymium shares three valence electrons; its three remaining unpaired 4f electrons stay on each atom and give strong magnetism in compounds."
source: Wikipedia Neodymium (Nd3+ is [Xe]4f3); standard lanthanide chemistry
reason: Nd is [Xe]4f4 6s2. If three electrons go into metallic bonding (as in Nd3+ and in Nd2Fe14B), three 4f electrons stay on each atom, not four. The sentence contradicts itself: 3 shared plus 4 kept would be 7 electrons beyond the Xe core, but Nd has only 6.

current: Iodine is a dark solid halogen that turns straight into violet vapor when warmed. Your thyroid needs it to make the hormones that control metabolism.
corrected: "Iodine is a dark solid halogen that gives off violet vapor when warmed and melts at 114 °C. Your thyroid needs it to make the hormones that control metabolism."
source: Wikipedia Iodine (sublimation demonstrations give rise to 'a misconception that it does not melt in atmospheric pressure'); triple point 386.65 K at 12.1 kPa
reason: At 1 atm, iodine melts at 113.7 °C and boils at 184 °C, matching this entry's own meltingPoint and boilingPoint. Saying it 'turns straight into' vapor repeats a well-known misconception. It sublimes appreciably below its melting point, but it does not skip the liquid phase.

current: Antimony is a brittle metalloid that, like water, expands slightly as it freezes, which made it valuable for casting sharp printing type.
corrected: "Antimony is a brittle metalloid that, added to lead, reduces shrinkage as the alloy freezes, which made it valuable for casting sharp printing type."
source: CRC/Wikipedia infobox densities (solid 6.69 g/cm3 near r.t., liquid 6.53 g/cm3 at m.p.); Wikipedia Type metal (antimony 'reduces shrinkage'); not in lists of substances that expand on freezing (water, Si, Ge, Ga, Bi, Pu)
reason: Antimony expanding on freezing is a popular claim, but the density data does not support it: liquid Sb at its melting point is less dense than the solid, so it most likely contracts slightly. The authoritative account of type metal is that antimony reduces the alloy's shrinkage, not that the element itself expands like water.

source: Johnson chart as encoded in Wikimedia Commons Nucleosynthesis_periodic_table.svg (Te: 57% dying low-mass stars, 43% merging neutron stars); s-only isotopes Te-122/123/124
reason: Johnson's chart gives Te a large dying-low-mass-star (s-process) share. Even residual-method estimates put s-process Te at about 20%, since Te-122, 123 and 124 are s-only. The category should be listed, as it is for Cs (15%) and Ce (24%).

current: Made almost entirely by rapid neutron capture.
corrected: "Made mostly by rapid neutron capture, with some slow capture in aging stars."

reason: 'Almost entirely' overstates the r-process share. The s-only isotopes Te-122, 123 and 124, plus part of Te-125 and Te-126, come from slow capture in AGB stars.

source: Johnson chart as encoded in Wikimedia Commons Nucleosynthesis_periodic_table.svg (Ba: 82% dying low-mass stars, 18% merging neutron stars)
reason: Johnson's chart gives about 18% of barium to merging neutron stars (r-process). Smaller minority shares are listed elsewhere in this dataset, for example Cs at 15% and Ce at 24%. The originNote already says 'mostly' slow capture.

current: Caesium is the most reactive stable metal. The second is defined by the vibrations of caesium-133 atoms: exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles.
corrected: "Caesium is the most reactive stable metal. The second is defined by microwaves that caesium-133 atoms absorb: exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles."
source: BIPM SI Brochure, definition of the second (ground-state hyperfine transition frequency of Cs-133)
reason: The second is defined by the frequency of the radiation from caesium-133's hyperfine transition, not by any physical vibration of the atoms. 'Vibrations of atoms' would mislead students into picturing atoms shaking.
